source.title: How Many Features Can a Language Model Store Under the Linear Representation Hypothesis?
source.authors: Nikhil Garg; Jon M. Kleinberg; Kenny Peng

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper derives theoretical bounds on sparse-feature storage under linear representation and linear accessibility, and refines the geometric account by showing that successful representations need not have the usual aligned, mutually orthogonal feature directions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports theoretical results, not measurements on trained language models or toy networks. Rows record its own bounds and constructions; results cited from prior work, including the classical compressed-sensing result, are not included.
record.test_reason: A purely theoretical paper. Its own proofs bound how many k-sparse features d dimensions can store under linear encoding and linear decoding. They also show which feature geometries this does and does not force, which bears on V1's capacity and geometry claims. It trains no network, so the result concerns what is possible, not what toy models actually learn.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that linear representation plus linear accessibility still allows exponentially many sparse features per neuron count, which they present as theoretical evidence for the superposition hypothesis. Linear accessibility needs roughly k² rather than k dependence, so it is strictly stronger than linear representation. Feature geometry is not pinned down: representation and probe directions can differ, with conventional alignment and orthogonality emerging under norm bounds.
record.recipe_differences: A mathematical framework and proof of capacity bounds and geometric constructions, rather than a trained toy-model optimization or empirical superposition measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: The geometric conclusions depend on whether representation and probe vector norms are bounded; the paper gives different constructions and constraints under those assumptions.
record.problems: The evidence is theoretical and depends on the paper's linear representation/accessibility framework and sparse-input assumptions; it does not establish that trained language models or toy networks use these constructions. The recovery-error condition in the supplied rendering of Theorem 3 is ambiguous.
record.rows_left_out: Theorem 1's classical compressed-sensing result is cited background, not a result of this study, so it is not recorded as a row.

untested.parts: No trained toy network is examined. The paper does not test the sparsity-dependent phase transition, feature importance, the specific regular polytope geometries, or whether gradient training finds these constructions.
Neuron polysemanticity and importance-based allocation of dimensions are not studied.
No LLM activations or SAE recovery are measured.
Remark 10 discusses SAE encoder and decoder directions but tests nothing about SAE features' completeness or stability.
Assumes 1-D features. Multidimensional features are only mentioned as future work.

missing.what: Corollary 13: adding a bias and monotonically increasing activation (e.g. ReLU, as in toy-model decoders) does not raise the Ω((k²/log k) log(m/k)) capacity bound. It is relevant to V1 because TMS uses ReLU readout. It is mentioned only in r9's note.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'challenges' label for r3–r5 is changed to limits_scope. An existence construction cannot show that the effect is absent where V1 says it holds in trained toy networks. The tests relation is marginal: all rows are proofs about a mathematical framework, not measurements of networks.

versions.untested_parts: No trained or toy network is tested. The paper does not test a sparsity-dependent transition, feature importance, or whether real networks adopt the constructed geometries.
Does not test neuron polysemanticity, allocation of dedicated dimensions to important features, or competition among features in a trained model.
Does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons.
No empirical LLM activations, neuron-distribution measurements, or SAE feature recovery are tested.
Discusses the distinction between representation and probe directions, but does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical.
The framework represents each feature with a vector, but the paper does not compare one-dimensional features with multidimensional features.

rows.subject: linear representation/accessibility framework

rows.note: The construction uses A = B with approximately orthogonal columns; the paper says this permits exponentially many features relative to embedding dimension.

rows.subject: linear representation/accessibility framework
rows.operation_detail: Constructs representations with distinct representation and probe directions.
rows.measure: Absolute cosine between a feature's representation vector and its probe vector
rows.value: For every i, |⟨a_i/||a_i||, b_i/||b_i||⟩| < δ + o(1)
rows.note: The construction permits a feature's own representation and probe directions to be almost orthogonal.
rows.check: This is an existence construction with untied encoder and decoder (A ≠ B). It shows near-orthogonal regular geometry is not required, not that trained networks lack it, so it is partial with respect to V1's geometry claim rather than observed.

rows.subject: linear representation/accessibility framework
rows.operation_detail: Constructs representations with highly aligned directions across different features.
rows.measure: Cosine between different features' representation vectors
rows.note: The result demonstrates that different representation vectors can be highly correlated while linear recovery still holds.
rows.check: Same as r3. Highly correlated representation directions are possible only in the untied, unbounded-norm setting. This is an existence result, not a measurement of a trained network.

rows.subject: linear representation/accessibility framework
rows.operation_detail: Constructs highly aligned probe directions across different features.
rows.measure: Cosine between different features' probe vectors
rows.note: The result demonstrates that different probe vectors can be highly correlated while linear recovery still holds.
rows.check: Same as r3, for probe directions.

rows.subject: linear representation/accessibility framework

rows.note: The paper concludes that bounded, unit-norm vectors align in the zero-error limit.

relationships.condition: Sparse inputs with linear encoding and linear decoding (theoretical capacity)
relationships.reason: Proves exponentially many k-sparse features fit in d = O(k² log m) via near-orthogonal tied directions (r1). The matching lower bound and binary-separation bound show capacity depends on sparsity k (r2, r9).
relationships.display_finding: Exponentially many k-sparse features fit in d = O(k² log m) dimensions using near-orthogonal tied directions. A matching lower bound and a binary-separation bound show that capacity depends on the sparsity k.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Representation and probe vectors with bounded (unit) norm, as in tied-weight toy models
source_check.reason: Proposition 11 establishes own representation/probe alignment and cross-feature near-orthogonality in the near-unit-norm, small-error limit. An arbitrary larger norm bound alone does not establish this geometry.

relationships.reason: Constructions show successful linear recovery with near-orthogonal own representation and probe directions and highly correlated cross-feature directions. Near-orthogonal geometry is therefore not implied by superposition itself (r3–r5). This is a possibility result, not evidence trained networks do this.
relationships.display_finding: Constructions recovered features linearly. Each feature's representation and probe directions were near-orthogonal to each other, but directions across features were highly correlated, so superposition need not imply near-orthogonal geometry. This is a possibility result, not evidence about trained networks.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: Proposition 9 constructs successful sparse recovery with highly correlated cross-feature directions and nearly orthogonal own representation/probe directions, qualifying any universal geometric implication of readable superposition.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Theoretical sparse linear-encoding and linear-recovery constructions
reader_labels.reason: The upper bound exhibits sparse feature storage with dimension growing as Oϵ(k² log m), and the lower bound and binary classification result provide corresponding capacity restrictions (r1, r2, r9).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Feature geometries allowed without additional norm constraints
reader_labels.reason: The paper constructs successful encodings with nearly orthogonal representation/probe vectors for the same feature and highly correlated directions across different features, so regular near-orthogonal geometry is not required (r3–r5).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The approximately aligned and mutually orthogonal geometry follows when vector norms are bounded, with the clean limit stated for unit norms and vanishing error; this qualifies the geometry result by its assumptions (r6–r8).
